title: UTF-8 BOM Python file is refused as 'syntax errors'
body:
The Python path decodes with 'utf-8' (not 'utf-8-sig') and passes the str to ast.parse. A leading U+FEFF in a str is an invalid non-printable character, so any valid BOM-prefixed .py (common for files saved by Windows editors) is refused. Verified: printf '\xef\xbb\xbfimport os
def f():
    pass
' > bom.py -> 'bom.py: syntax errors — read the file instead', exit 1. python3 itself runs the file fine.
fix: Decode with 'utf-8-sig' and errors='replace' (or strip a leading '\ufeff'). Add a BOM fixture to the Python tests.

title: RecursionError from ast.parse escapes as a traceback instead of a refusal
body: _python_entries catches only SyntaxError and ValueError. Deeply nested but valid code, such as generated source or a long chained expression, makes ast.parse raise RecursionError ('maximum recursion depth exceeded during ast construction'). The CLI then dies with a Python traceback and prints no '<path>: <reason>' line, which breaks the 'exactly one line, exit 1, never an empty body' contract. Verified: a 1 MB file 'x = 1+1+...+1' (200 000 terms, well under max_bytes) gives a traceback. ast.unparse on the resulting nodes has the same exposure.
fix: Catch RecursionError (and MemoryError) around ast.parse and around entry building, and refuse with e.g. 'syntax errors — read the file instead' or a dedicated 'too deeply nested' reason.

title: Unreadable file (PermissionError or other OSError) crashes with a traceback
body: The only handler in skeleton() is 'except _Refusal'. real.stat() and real.read_bytes() can raise PermissionError, and other OSErrors such as EIO or a file removed between is_file and read. These propagate as a traceback with no refusal line. Verified: chmod 000 noperm.py; klc skeleton noperm.py -> PermissionError traceback. For a non-Python file, the unreadable case goes to ast-grep, which reports it as skipped, so it becomes a misleading 'unsupported language'.
fix: Wrap the stat and read calls in 'except OSError as e: raise _Refusal(f"cannot read: {e.strerror}")' (or reuse 'not a file'), and add a refusal test for it.

title: Non-UTF-8 non-Python file is reported as 'unsupported language: .ts'
body: ast-grep 0.42.1 skips a file it cannot decode as UTF-8. Its stderr then has 'summary|file: scannedFileCount=1,skippedFileCount=1' and no entity|file line, so the code refuses with 'unsupported language: .ts' even though the profile clearly covers TypeScript. This is a dishonest label, and it also contradicts the spec's encoding assumption ('decoded with errors=replace, and the outline is still produced'). Verified with a .ts file containing a raw 0xE9 byte in an identifier. The same misleading reason comes up when the path contains a newline, because the entity line is split across two stderr lines and _ENTITY_RE never matches.
fix: Parse skippedFileCount from the summary|file line. When it is at least 1 and there is no entity line, refuse with 'ast-grep failed (file skipped: not UTF-8 or unreadable) — read the file instead' rather than 'unsupported language'. Alternatively, check the bytes decode as UTF-8 before the call. Add a non-UTF-8 fixture test.

title: Header line count uses str.splitlines(), which disagrees with ast line numbers
body:
str.splitlines() also splits on \x0c (form feed, common in older Python sources), \x1c-\x1e, \x85,   and  , while ast and editors count only 
, 
 and . Verified: 'import os
\x0c
def f():
    pass
' (4 lines) gets the header '(python, 5 lines)', and a   inside a string literal inflates it too. Ranges are unaffected, but the header can point past the file's end.
fix: Count with len(text.splitlines()) only after normalising, or use something like text.count('\n') + (not text.endswith('\n')), adjusted for lone \r.

title: ast-grep output is decoded with the locale encoding (text=True, no encoding=)
body: subprocess.run(..., text=True) decodes ast-grep's UTF-8 JSON and stderr with locale.getpreferredencoding(). On Windows (the repo ships klc-completion.ps1) that is often cp1252. Non-ASCII match text or paths then turn into mojibake, or raise an uncaught UnicodeDecodeError for bytes that cp1252 does not define (0x81, 0x8D, 0x8F, 0x90, 0x9D), which is a traceback rather than a refusal. On Linux in UTF-8 mode this is fine, and deterministic_inventory has the same pattern.

title: No '--' separator, so a path beginning with '-' cannot be passed conventionally
body: main() treats every argv element as the path and requires exactly one. 'klc skeleton -- -x.ts' prints usage and exits 2. 'klc skeleton -x.ts' happens to work, and it is safe because ast-grep receives the resolved absolute path, so there is no flag injection. The standard '--' idiom is still rejected, though.
fix: Drop a leading '--' before the argument-count check.
